paragraphs: This paper studies optimization when the function being minimized is smooth and strongly convex, but its gradients may be noisy. The challenge is to make rapid progress while controlling the effects of unreliable gradient estimates. An algorithm suited to exact gradients also needs to handle noise without letting that noise undermine its convergence.

The proposed method organizes accelerated optimization into multiple stages. Each stage uses a stochastic version of Nesterov’s method, with a particular restart scheme and carefully chosen parameters. These choices target the bias and variance terms in the convergence bounds: the method coordinates progress toward the optimum with control over the contribution from gradient noise.

The central result is optimal convergence rates in both deterministic and stochastic settings, without requiring knowledge of the noise characteristics. Here, “universally optimal” refers to these two settings within the stated smooth, strongly convex problem class. The contribution is a staged acceleration strategy that achieves the appropriate rate whether gradients are exact or noisy.
neurips-2019-a-universally-optimal-multi.tldr: A multistage accelerated optimizer achieves optimal rates for smooth, strongly convex objectives with or without gradient noise, without knowing the noise characteristics.

paragraphs: Few-shot image classification asks a model to learn new categories from very few labeled examples. This paper extends metric-based approaches by bringing together visual features and semantic representations learned from unlabeled text. The motivation is that images and language offer different kinds of evidence, and their usefulness can vary across categories.

The proposed mechanism adjusts how it combines the two modalities according to the new image categories being learned. Some concepts may be easier to distinguish visually, while others benefit more from semantic information. Text representations can also supply prior knowledge and context when the available images provide weak support. Adaptive combination lets the model vary its emphasis instead of assigning both sources a fixed role.

Across all benchmarks and few-shot settings tested, the authors report large improvements over single-modality methods and methods based on aligning modalities. Their experiments also show that the model changes its focus between visual and semantic information. The largest gains occur with especially few examples, supporting the usefulness of semantic context when visual evidence is scarce.
neurips-2019-adaptive-cross-modal-few-sh.tldr: Adaptively combining image features with text-derived semantics improves few-shot classification, especially when labeled examples are very scarce.

paragraphs: Computing the permanent of a non-negative matrix is a difficult counting problem with applications including tracking and statistical thermodynamics. Although a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme exists, the abstract describes it as impractical and difficult to implement. This paper introduces ADAPART to make sampling and approximation more usable.

ADAPART samples permutations exactly according to weights defined by a matrix. It repeatedly adapts a partition of the permutation space, turning an upper-bounding method for the permanent into one with the required nesting property across that partition. The resulting samples support tight bounds on the permanent that hold with high probability. Exactness applies to the sampling procedure; the permanent itself is bounded probabilistically.

Experiments show substantial speedups over earlier work, sometimes exceeding fiftyfold. The authors also observe polynomial scaling in some cases, an empirical finding rather than a general runtime guarantee. In multi-target tracking, the method enables an optimal proposal distribution for particle filtering, yielding orders of magnitude fewer samples and better tracking performance.
neurips-2019-approximating-the-permanent.tldr: ADAPART uses adaptive partitions to sample weighted permutations exactly and build high-probability permanent bounds, with substantial empirical speedups.

paragraphs: This paper examines how people think tasks should be shared between humans and AI. Technical capability alone does not answer how much control people want to delegate. The authors develop a human-centered framework around four factors that may shape these decisions: motivation, difficulty, risk, and trust.

To study preferences empirically, they assemble 100 tasks drawn from academic papers, portrayals of AI in popular media, and everyday life. They then conduct a survey using the framework. This connects the abstract question of delegation to judgments about concrete tasks, allowing the authors to examine how preferences relate to the four proposed factors.

Survey responses show little preference for complete AI control and a strong preference for arrangements in which humans lead with machine assistance. Trust has the strongest correlation with delegation preferences among the four factors; this finding does not establish that trust causes those preferences. The authors present the framework as an initial characterization of human attitudes intended to inform discussion and research, rather than prescribe a direction for technology development.
neurips-2019-ask-not-what-ai-can-do-but-.tldr: A survey-based delegation framework finds a preference for human-led AI assistance, with trust most strongly correlated with delegation preferences.

paragraphs: A generative model can produce samples whose statistics differ from those of the data it aims to represent. This paper addresses that discrepancy through importance weighting: generated samples receive different weights so that their contributions better reflect the underlying data distribution. The usual obstacle is that the required likelihood ratio may be unknown.

The authors estimate this ratio using a probabilistic classifier trained to distinguish model-generated samples from samples of the data distribution. This turns a discrimination problem into a way to obtain correction weights without directly evaluating the relevant likelihoods. The approach therefore applies importance weighting even when the ratio needed by the standard procedure is unavailable.

Experiments consistently improve standard goodness-of-fit measures for samples from state-of-the-art deep generative models. The authors interpret these improvements as evidence suggesting reduced bias. They also demonstrate usefulness in two settings: augmenting classification data with generative adversarial networks, and evaluating policies through a model using off-policy data. These applications show how correction weights can matter beyond assessing generated sample quality.
neurips-2019-bias-correction-of-learned-.tldr: Classifier-estimated importance weights improve generative-model goodness-of-fit measures and support bias correction in downstream applications.

paragraphs: Convolutional networks pass feature maps from one layer to the next. This paper focuses on a different opportunity for information exchange: explicit communication among channels within a layer. Treating each convolutional filter as a neuron, the authors ask whether those neurons can improve their representations by considering one another’s responses before passing information onward.

Their Cross-channel Communication, or C3, block provides that exchange through a small neural network. It contains a feature encoder, a message communicator, and a feature decoder. Together, these components let each neuron account for responses from other channels at the same level. The intended result is features that distinguish inputs more effectively and complement the information represented by other channels.

Experiments across multiple computer vision tasks show that this mechanism lets shallower networks combine useful information within individual layers. The tested networks outperform baseline deep networks and other competitive methods. These findings support explicit within-layer communication as a useful architectural choice alongside the established practice of increasing network depth.
neurips-2019-cross-channel-communication.tldr: C3 blocks let convolutional channels exchange information within a layer, helping shallower networks outperform deeper baselines in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to improve robustness by training a model on deliberately perturbed examples. Conventional approaches often use supervised objectives to create those perturbations. This paper highlights label leaking as a problem with such attack-generation schemes and proposes a different way to construct adversarial training images.

The method creates perturbations through feature scattering in the model’s latent representation space. Its attack-generation procedure is unsupervised, which the authors state avoids label leaking. It also constructs perturbed images collaboratively, taking relationships between samples into account. The generation process therefore uses information about how examples relate to one another, rather than treating each image solely as an isolated attack target.

The paper analyzes model robustness and reports extensive experiments on different datasets, including comparisons with state-of-the-art approaches. Those experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed training method. The contribution combines two ideas in adversarial example generation: working through latent features without supervision and using inter-sample relationships to guide the perturbations used during training.
neurips-2019-defense-against-adversarial.tldr: Feature scattering generates adversarial training images without supervision while accounting for relationships between samples, improving robustness in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Sorting and ranking appear throughout machine learning, but their ordinary forms fit poorly into gradient-based training. Ranks are discrete, and sorting values involves changes in their ordering. This paper constructs smooth substitutes so that operations based on ordering can participate in automatically differentiated learning pipelines.

The starting point is to view sorting as an assignment problem: input values are matched to an increasing collection of target values. The authors extend this view using optimal transport, which relaxes the assignment formulation. Their generalized operators allow a weighted target distribution whose number of support points can differ from the number of inputs, expanding the construction beyond ordinary one-to-one sorting.

An entropy penalty smooths the transport problem, and Sinkhorn iterations solve the resulting formulation. This produces differentiable rank and sort operators. The authors use them to construct smooth proxies for classification’s zero-one loss and for quantile regression loss. The contribution provides a way to express ordering-based objectives in a form compatible with end-to-end gradient optimization.
neurips-2019-differentiable-ranking-and-.tldr: Entropy-regularized optimal transport turns sorting and ranking into differentiable proxies usable in gradient-based learning objectives.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits repeatedly choose among actions using available context and learn from the resulting rewards. Many algorithms become harder to use effectively as the number of context features grows. This paper considers stochastic linear contextual bandits where the context is high-dimensional but only a small subset of features is associated with reward.

The proposed Doubly-Robust Lasso Bandit combines sparse regression with a doubly robust technique from missing-data research. Lasso supplies the mechanism for exploiting sparsity in the regression parameter. Combining these ideas addresses a setting where a large feature description contains only a much smaller amount of reward-relevant information.

The authors establish a high-probability regret upper bound that depends logarithmically on the context dimension and does not depend on the number of arms. This improves the dimensional dependence relative to polynomial dependence described for many existing algorithms. They also report good performance when contexts across different arms are correlated and fewer tuning parameters than existing methods. These benefits are stated for the sparse stochastic linear setting studied.
neurips-2019-doubly-robust-lasso-bandit-.tldr: Combining Lasso with doubly robust estimation yields a sparse linear bandit algorithm with logarithmic dimensional dependence in its high-probability regret bound.

paragraphs: This paper studies probability models for selecting subsets while expressing preferences about diversity. Strongly Rayleigh distributions, including determinantal point processes, provide elegant diversity models, but the authors argue that their diversity behavior is difficult to control intuitively. They propose strongly log-concave distributions as a more flexible modeling class.

Strongly log-concave distributions strictly include the strongly Rayleigh family. The authors illustrate how this broader class permits easier control over diversity through practically relevant examples. To make the models usable for learning and inference, they develop tools for two different tasks: drawing random subsets from the distribution and finding a mode, meaning a most probable subset.

For sampling, the paper supplies a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm with theoretical mixing-time bounds, which characterize convergence toward the target distribution. For mode finding, it establishes a weak log-submodularity property and uses that property to obtain optimization guarantees for a distorted greedy algorithm. These results connect greater modeling flexibility with algorithms supported by theory.
neurips-2019-flexible-modeling-of-divers.tldr: Strongly log-concave distributions offer more controllable diversity models, supported by sampling bounds and guarantees for greedy mode finding.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks combine node attributes with connections between nodes, repeatedly passing information along edges. This combination makes predictions difficult to interpret because both the graph structure and the features can matter. GNNExplainer addresses this problem with a model-agnostic method for explaining predictions from GNN-based models.

For an individual prediction, the method seeks a compact subgraph and a small set of node features that play a crucial role in the result. It formulates this search as an optimization problem that maximizes mutual information between the prediction and a distribution over possible subgraphs. The approach can also produce concise, consistent explanations for a whole class of instances.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world graphs show that GNNExplainer identifies important structures and features, with an average improvement of 17.1% over the evaluated baselines. The explanations can expose meaningful graph patterns and provide insight into model errors. Their practical value is to make the structural and feature evidence behind predictions easier to inspect.
neurips-2019-gnnexplainer-generating-exp.tldr: GNNExplainer identifies compact subgraphs and node features that explain GNN predictions, outperforming evaluated explanation baselines.

paragraphs: Causal effect identification asks whether observational data and a specified causal structure uniquely determine the distribution produced by an intervention. This paper considers additional information in the form of context-specific independence: independence relationships that hold in particular contexts. Existing identification methods based on do-calculus are incomplete when these relationships are present.

The authors first show that deciding non-identifiability in the presence of context-specific independence is NP-hard. They then develop a calculus and an automated search procedure that use these relationships to identify causal effects. The calculus includes standard do-calculus as a special case, extending the reasoning tools available for deriving intervention formulas.

The approach is provably sound, meaning its derivations justify the effects it identifies. Soundness does not itself claim that the search can identify every identifiable effect. The authors obtain formulas unavailable to previous procedures and show that even a small number of context-specific independence relations may make a previously non-identifiable instance identifiable. Such information can therefore change what causal conclusions observational evidence supports.
neurips-2019-identifying-causal-effects-.tldr: A sound extension of do-calculus uses context-specific independence to identify causal effects beyond the reach of previous procedures.

paragraphs: In bandit combinatorial optimization, a player selects a binary action vector and incurs a loss determined by an unobserved loss vector. The paper asks which properties of those losses make learning difficult. Its focus is regret and how its unavoidable size depends on dimension d, maximum action size k, and number of rounds T.

The authors strengthen an earlier regret lower bound to order √(dk³T), removing a logarithmic gap. Their construction uses strongly correlated losses that take binary values. This demonstrates that continuous-valued losses are unnecessary for obtaining the stronger difficulty result. The bound also yields improved results for multitask, ranking, and multiple-play bandits, resolving the cited open problem for bandit ranking.

The paper then contrasts correlated losses with the case where entries of the loss vector are independent random variables. Under that independence condition, regret of order √(dk²T), up to logarithmic factors, is achievable. The comparison identifies correlations among losses as a source of the larger regret, with a √k separation in the main scaling.
neurips-2019-improved-regret-bounds-for-.tldr: A stronger regret lower bound shows how correlated binary losses make combinatorial bandits harder than the independent-loss setting.

paragraphs: A single training-loss value summarizes the behavior of a neural network with many changing parameters. Loss Change Allocation, or LCA, provides a more detailed view by assigning portions of the loss change to individual parameters. This reveals which parameter movements contribute to decreasing the loss and which contribute to increasing it.

The method decomposes an approximate path integral along the training trajectory using a Runge-Kutta integrator. Its allocation conservatively partitions the change in loss across parameters. Those contributions can then be added across training iterations or grouped by neurons, channels, and layers, allowing the same measurement to support both detailed and broader views of training.

The reported observations challenge a picture of uniform progress: barely more than half of parameters help during a given iteration, and some entire layers hurt overall. The authors hypothesize that phase lag in oscillatory training may explain the latter finding. They also observe synchronized learning increments across layers, often peaking together. LCA thus exposes coordinated and opposing contributions hidden by the aggregate loss.
neurips-2019-lca-loss-change-allocation-.tldr: LCA allocates training-loss changes to parameters, revealing opposing contributions and synchronized patterns across neural-network layers.

paragraphs: Matrix completion can become biased when observed entries are unrepresentative of missing ones. For example, users may preferentially rate items they like, leading a method that assumes uniform observation to overestimate unseen ratings. This paper estimates entry-observation probabilities so that existing completion methods can correct for this selection pattern.

The key input is the binary matrix recording whether each entry is revealed. Unlike the original values, this observation mask is fully available. Motivated by low nuclear norm structure in real missingness patterns, the authors apply an existing nuclear-norm-constrained matrix completion algorithm to this mask. They first recover missingness probabilities, then use those estimates to debias losses for completing the original matrix.

The paper provides finite-sample error bounds for both probability estimation and the resulting correction of completion losses. Experiments show improvements across several existing algorithms. Downstream accuracy is at least as good as the tested logistic-regression and naive-Bayes debiasing baselines, which require additional auxiliary information. The approach replaces those modeling choices with the stated low nuclear norm structural assumption.
neurips-2019-missing-not-at-random-in-ma.tldr: Estimating missingness probabilities from a structured observation mask helps debias matrix completion, with finite-sample guarantees and empirical improvements.

paragraphs: Neural translation systems commonly generate a sentence in one direction, which limits their use of global information about the target sentence. Earlier two-pass approaches try to supply that information but face quality and efficiency limitations. This paper introduces a soft prototype into the encoder-decoder framework to give generation a broader view of the translation.

The prototype gives the decoder indirect access to information about both earlier and later target content. Each word can therefore be generated with more global context than one-directional decoding alone provides. The authors also develop an efficient method for producing the prototype, addressing the practical cost of adding this source of information.

Experiments across translation tasks show significant generation-quality improvements over the baseline with little additional storage or inference time. The paper reports state-of-the-art results on the WMT2014, WMT2015, and WMT2017 English-to-German tasks. These findings support the usefulness of the prototype as a way to improve target-side context while keeping its added computational cost small in the evaluated systems.
neurips-2019-neural-machine-translation-.tldr: A soft target-sentence prototype gives translation decoders indirect past and future context, improving quality with little additional storage or inference time.

paragraphs: RobinHood is an offline contextual bandit algorithm designed to learn decision policies subject to fairness constraints. The paper treats the choice of fairness definition as part of the problem specification. Users can provide multiple definitions or construct definitions tailored to the application, allowing the method to accommodate a broad family of requirements.

The theoretical contribution is a probabilistic guarantee about the policy returned by the algorithm. The probability that RobinHood returns an unfair solution is bounded by a threshold chosen by the user. This gives an explicit way to control the risk of violating the supplied fairness requirements, rather than relying solely on observed performance during evaluation.

The authors evaluate RobinHood in tutoring, loan approval, and criminal recidivism settings. The tutoring application includes a user study and multiple distinct fairness definitions; the other applications use the specified credit and recidivism datasets. In each setting, the algorithm produces fair policies with performance competitive with other offline and online contextual bandit algorithms. The results demonstrate the approach across differing applications and fairness specifications.
neurips-2019-offline-contextual-bandits-.tldr: RobinHood learns offline bandit policies while bounding the probability of returning a solution that violates user-specified fairness constraints.

paragraphs: Adding stack-like memory to recurrent neural networks offers a way to represent structured computations, but training such memory models has been difficult. Ordered Memory addresses this problem with an architecture that explicitly controls memory updates and builds higher-level representations from lower-level ones. The design is inspired by the Ordered Neurons approach.

A new attention mechanism governs memory operations through cumulative probabilities. These probabilities control writing and erasing, providing a coordinated mechanism for changing the stored information. A Gated Recursive Cell supplies the complementary composition operation, combining lower-level representations into higher-level representations. Together, the components link memory management with the construction of hierarchical structure.

The authors report strong results on logical inference and ListOps, and performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods on Stanford Sentiment Treebank tasks. They also interpret the model to recover its induced tree structures and find alignment with the ground truth. This structural agreement provides evidence that the model’s internal organization captures relevant hierarchy alongside achieving useful task performance.
neurips-2019-ordered-memory-142933230d.tldr: Ordered Memory combines attention-controlled memory updates with recursive composition, achieving strong task results and induced trees aligned with ground truth.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic bandits with a continuous space of possible actions. The objective function’s smoothness influences how effectively an algorithm can learn where to act, but that smoothness may be unknown. The central question is how much regret must be paid for adapting to this missing knowledge.

The authors focus on Hölder regularity, a way of describing smoothness, and establish a polynomial cost of adaptation for regret minimization. They revisit an existing lower bound and define admissible rate functions. These functions describe achievable patterns of regret rates across different regularity levels, making the tradeoffs involved in adaptation explicit.

They then introduce an algorithm that adapts to unknown smoothness and matches any of the characterized minimal rate functions. The analysis includes finite-time guarantees and a discussion of asymptotic optimality. The result pairs a description of the cost of adaptation with an algorithm that meets the corresponding optimal tradeoffs, clarifying what can be achieved without knowing the objective’s regularity in advance.
neurips-2019-polynomial-cost-of-adaptati.tldr: The paper characterizes the polynomial regret cost of adapting to unknown smoothness in continuum-armed bandits and gives an algorithm matching optimal tradeoffs.

paragraphs: Substring kernels are established ways to represent biological sequences and text, while neural networks offer end-to-end learning when labeled data is available. This paper develops a connection between these approaches. Its goal is to retain a kernel-based foundation while obtaining a recurrent model whose representation can be trained for a task.

The authors generalize convolutional kernel networks to handle gaps in sequences. This extension produces a new kind of recurrent neural network, building on the relationship between sequence kernels and recurrent computation. The resulting model supports two training routes: supervised end-to-end learning through backpropagation and unsupervised learning through kernel approximation techniques.

These alternatives make the same model family relevant to settings with and without supervision. The empirical evaluation focuses on biological sequences, where the method outperforms existing approaches on protein classification tasks. The findings support the suitability of the proposed sequence representation for those tasks and show that modeling gaps within a kernel-derived recurrent architecture can be effective.
neurips-2019-recurrent-kernel-networks-b.tldr: Recurrent kernel networks model sequence gaps and support supervised or unsupervised training, outperforming existing methods on evaluated protein classification tasks.

paragraphs: Continuous-time Bayesian networks model interacting variables that evolve over time. Complete observations permit efficient estimation, but incomplete data require reasoning about hidden states. Learning the network structure makes this especially expensive because the space of possible structures grows super-exponentially, and separately evaluating candidates entails costly latent-state estimation.

The paper replaces individual structure sampling and scoring with a gradient-based formulation. It assumes that the network’s generator is a mixture of generators associated with different structures. Structure learning then becomes optimization of the mixture weights. This changes how candidate structures enter the learning problem, allowing their contributions to be adjusted through continuous optimization.

A new variational method complements this formulation by enabling closed-form calculation of the mixture marginal likelihood within the framework. The authors demonstrate scalability on synthetic and real-world data, learning structures of sizes they describe as previously inaccessible. The contribution addresses both the representation of structure choices and the inference calculation needed to learn from incomplete observations.
neurips-2019-scalable-structure-learning.tldr: A mixture-of-generators formulation and variational inference enable scalable gradient-based structure learning for continuous-time Bayesian networks with incomplete data.

paragraphs: Point processes describe events occurring over time, and learning from their histories can be computationally expensive. This paper proposes thinning as a downsampling strategy to accelerate that learning. The objective is to use a reduced event history while retaining enough information to estimate the process effectively.

The authors find that thinning preserves the structure of the intensity, which describes the process’s event rate. They develop theoretical results for estimating intensities, parameters, and gradients from a thinned history. Those results apply to point processes with decouplable intensities, a stated condition on the class of models covered by the theory.

The paper also introduces a stochastic optimization algorithm driven by the thinned gradient. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support thinning for parameter estimation, gradient estimation, and optimization. The reported outcome is reduced estimation time without much accuracy loss. Together, the structural results and experiments explain how downsampling can serve as a computational tool for learning these processes, rather than merely reducing the amount of stored data.
neurips-2019-thinning-for-accelerating-t.tldr: Thinning accelerates point-process estimation and optimization with little reported accuracy loss, with theory for decouplable intensities.

paragraphs: Meta-reinforcement learning uses experience across tasks to learn how to learn quickly. Its training tasks are often manually designed, which can require substantial effort. This paper develops an unsupervised method that discovers and updates a training-task distribution through interaction with a visual environment.

A parametric density model of the learner’s trajectories supports the evolving curriculum. The objective maximizes information between a latent task variable and the learner’s data distribution. In practice, the method alternates between incorporating recent experience into the task distribution and meta-learning on the revised tasks. Repeating these steps reorganizes the curriculum as the learner’s experience changes. Discriminative clustering of visual representations supports task acquisition and exploration at the trajectory level.

Experiments use navigation and manipulation environments with visual observations. The learned behavior transfers to downstream tasks defined by manually designed reward functions, and the unsupervised training also improves the efficiency of subsequent meta-learning on test-task distributions. These results support automatic curriculum discovery as useful preparation for later tasks, even when their rewards are specified separately.
neurips-2019-unsupervised-curricula-for-.tldr: An unsupervised curriculum adapts tasks to a visual meta-RL learner’s experience and supports downstream transfer and more efficient later meta-learning.

paragraphs: Learning from video requires understanding both what is present and how it moves. This paper tackles that problem without supervision by representing images through keypoints and learning a stochastic model of how those keypoints evolve. The representation gives motion an explicit spatial form that can support prediction and object-level understanding.

Future frames are reconstructed from predicted keypoints together with a reference frame. Modeling the dynamics in keypoint coordinates produces stable learning and avoids compounding errors in pixel space, according to the authors. This separates the representation of motion from the reconstruction of detailed images while retaining a path back to pixel-level video predictions.

The evaluation spans multi-agent sports, Human3.6M, and continuous-control datasets from the DeepMind Control Suite. The method improves on unstructured representations for video prediction and downstream motion tasks, including object tracking, action recognition, and reward prediction. These results indicate that the learned spatial structure is useful beyond reconstructing frames: it also captures motion information relevant to several forms of subsequent analysis.
neurips-2019-unsupervised-learning-of-ob.tldr: Learning stochastic keypoint dynamics from unlabeled video improves frame prediction and motion-related tasks over unstructured representations.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimal experimental design aims to make limited experimental resources more informative. A central quantity is expected information gain, which expresses how much an experiment is expected to teach us. Accurately estimating that quantity can be difficult enough to restrict the practical use of the design framework.

This paper introduces several classes of fast information-gain estimators based on ideas from amortized variational inference. The contribution targets the calculation needed to assess candidate experiments. Improving this calculation matters because experiment selection depends on estimates that are both informative and affordable to compute, especially when experimental resources themselves are constrained.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that their estimators can substantially improve speed and accuracy over previous approaches. They also demonstrate the method in multiple end-to-end experiments, supporting its practicality within the full design process. The stated result is that these estimators can make Bayesian experimental design more usable by improving a central computational step; it is not a claim that every estimator improves every experimental setting.
neurips-2019-variational-bayesian-optima.tldr: Variational information-gain estimators can make Bayesian experimental design faster and more accurate, with theoretical and end-to-end empirical support.
